I've been farming these 7 mu for 35 years, since my father handed me the hoe when I was 18. Six mouths to feed at home, and my son only comes back from his construction job in Handan for harvest, so it's mostly me and my wife doing the work. I can't afford to gamble — steady is better than sorry.

I plant wheat on all seven mu every year. It's our staple, the straw feeds our goats, and I know this crop like the back of my hand. For seed, I buy the improved variety from Lao Zhang's supply shop, the one in the yellow bag. Not the expensive hybrid wheat — costs too much and you can't save seed. I spread compound fertilizer at planting, about one bag for every three mu, then topdress urea when the wheat greens up and again at jointing. My neighbor Li does the same and his wheat always looks better than mine if I skimp. That works out to roughly 16 kg of nitrogen per mu total — I don't weigh it, but Lao Zhang calculated it once when I asked. I irrigate three times from the well: right after sowing so the seedlings survive winter, once at jointing in March, and once when the grain is filling in May. Pumping costs electricity, so three times is enough. I spray three times too — herbicide after planting, then insecticide or fungicide in spring if I see aphids or rust. I rotary till before wheat every year; the soil is loamy and doesn't need deep plowing.

After cutting wheat in early June, I have less than a week to get maize in before the season slips away. Everyone uses hybrid maize seed now — the old local type can't compete. I plant right into the wheat stubble with no tillage, sometimes just a quick rotary pass if the stubble is thick, because there's no time to plow properly. Maize gets a bit less fertilizer than wheat, about 15 kg nitrogen per mu, because the wheat already pulled a lot from the soil and I have to watch my costs. I irrigate twice — once after sowing if it's dry, and once at the big ear stage in August when rain might not come. Two pesticide sprays: herbicide at planting, and insecticide if corn borers show up. If the summer storms don't flatten it, I expect about 520 kg per mu from the maize, and about 480 kg from the wheat.
